alternatives.label: Do nothing
alternatives.narrative: You can choose not to have treatment. Symptoms may stay the same, improve, or worsen. Over time, skin changes and ulcers can develop in some people and may become irreversible.

alternatives.label: Compression stockings
alternatives.narrative: Medical-grade compression stockings can relieve symptoms but do not make varicose veins go away. They need to be fitted professionally and replaced every 3–6 months.

alternatives.label: Other endovenous treatments
alternatives.narrative: Other keyhole options include endovenous laser ablation, cyanoacrylate glue closure, and mechanochemical ablation. Outcomes are broadly similar; your surgeon can advise which suits your vein pattern.

alternatives.label: Open surgery (tie and stripping)
alternatives.narrative: The traditional operation ties off and removes the faulty vein through a cut in the groin. It is effective but usually needs a general anaesthetic and has a longer recovery than keyhole options.

alternatives.label: Open vein surgery
alternatives.narrative: The traditional open operation involves a cut in the groin, tying off the faulty vein and removing it. It is effective but generally requires a general anaesthetic and has a longer recovery than keyhole options.

alternatives.label: Lifestyle measures
alternatives.narrative: Regular walking, leg elevation when resting, weight management, and avoiding long periods of standing still can help control symptoms but will not remove varicose veins.

benefits.label: Relief from aching and heavy legs
benefits.narrative: Most people notice that the aching, throbbing, and heavy feeling in the leg gets better after treatment. Around 80–85 in every 100 patients report improvement in symptoms.

benefits.label: Reduced leg and ankle swelling
benefits.narrative: Swelling in the lower leg and around the ankle, especially later in the day, usually improves after the faulty veins are closed.

benefits.label: Reduced risk of skin damage and ulcers
benefits.narrative: Untreated varicose veins can cause brown staining, eczema, and hardening of the skin, which may become permanent. Between 1 and 5 in every 100 people with varicose veins develop a leg ulcer during their lifetime. Treatment reduces this risk.

benefits.label: Improved appearance of the legs
benefits.narrative: Bulging surface veins usually flatten and become much less visible over the weeks following treatment.

complications.label: Bruising
complications.narrative: Bruising along the treated vein is common and settles over about three weeks. Around 25 in every 100 people notice it.

complications.label: Leg pain for 1–2 weeks
complications.narrative: Pulling or aching discomfort in the treated leg typically lasts 1–2 weeks and is usually controlled with simple painkillers. About 15–20 in every 100 people experience this.

complications.label: Inflammation of the treated vein (phlebitis)
complications.narrative: Firm, tender, red cords along the treated vein are a normal part of healing for some people and settle over a few weeks with anti-inflammatories and a warm compress.

complications.label: Pins and needles or numbness (short-term)
complications.narrative: A patch of numbness or pins and needles in the skin over the treated area, usually settling within 6 weeks. Around 5 in every 100 people notice this.

complications.label: Persistent numbness beyond 6 months
complications.narrative: Rarely (fewer than 1 in every 100 people) an area of numbness does not fully recover and may be permanent.

complications.label: Nerve injury causing foot drop
complications.narrative: The nerve that supplies movement of the foot can very rarely be damaged causing an inability to raise the foot up.

complications.label: Blood clot in the leg or lung (DVT / PE)
complications.narrative: After any operation, especially if you are less mobile while recovering, a blood clot (deep vein thrombosis) can form in the deep veins of the leg. Occasionally part of the clot travels to the lungs (pulmonary embolism), which can be serious. The risk depends on the type of operation and your individual risk factors, and is reduced by early walking, compression stockings, and where appropriate blood-thinning injections.

complications.label: Varicose veins coming back
complications.narrative: Varicose veins can come back within five years in 15–25 of every 100 people treated. If they do, further treatment is usually possible.

procedures.name: Radiofrequency ablation of single venous trunk +/- phlebectomies - unilateral
procedures.narrative: Heat is delivered through a thin catheter inside the faulty surface vein in one leg to seal it from the inside. This is usually done under local anaesthetic through a small puncture; varicose tributaries may be removed through tiny skin nicks at the same sitting.
